heading: What is a Trappist?
credit: Aubry de La Mottraye, 1727 · Wikimedia Commons, public domain
text: Trappists are monks and nuns of the Order of Cistercians of the Strict Observance (OCSO) – an independent Catholic order since 1892, which emerged from the Cistercians who follow the Rule of Saint Benedict. Their life is centred on silence, prayer and work, lived in secluded monastic communities.

heading: Origins: La Trappe, 1664
credit: Portrait of Armand-Jean de Rancé, Musée Condé · Wikimedia Commons, public domain
text: Armand Jean le Bouthillier de Rancé, at first abbot of La Trappe in Normandy in title only, turned his back on court life and reformed the abbey from the ground up in 1664: strict penance, silence, hard labour, simple food. Other Cistercian monasteries adopted the reform – and with it the name “Trappists”.

heading: Philosophy: Prayer and Work
credit: Achel Abbey, 1946 · Wikimedia Commons, public domain
text: At the heart of Trappist life is the balance of prayer and work, often summed up as “Ora et Labora” – although this exact wording was coined only in the 19th century and does not appear in the original Rule of Benedict. Among Trappists, silence is not a strict vow but a lived restraint: meals are taken together and in quiet, accompanied by a reading.

heading: Spread and Exile
credit: Memorial plaque for Dom Augustin de Lestrange, Lyon · Wikimedia Commons, CC0
text: In 1792, during the French Revolution, La Trappe was expropriated and the monks were driven out. Under Dom Augustin de Lestrange they found a new home at Val-Sainte in Switzerland – until 1798, when the next departure followed: a two-year odyssey through Germany, Austria, Bohemia and Poland as far as Russia, where Tsar Paul I had invited them. In 1800 they had to move on from there too, across the Baltic Sea to Lübeck. Only after the Napoleonic Wars did the communities return to France.

heading: Craft and Self-Sufficiency
credit: Tre Fontane Abbey, Rome, 1902 · Wikimedia Commons, public domain
text: Benedictine monasteries are meant to be able to support themselves – hard physical work is part of spiritual life, not merely a means to an end. In many places this gave rise to the craft of brewing: Westmalle first brewed for its own use in 1836, Orval from 1931 to finance the rebuilding of the destroyed abbey. Beer became part of the monastic economy – not its centrepiece.
